subject: A question about the Change Point Model example in the manual

messages.author: 75fd0d484a6132fa
messages.subject: A question about the Change Point Model example in the manual
parts:
Hello,

I am a little confused after reading the subsection "Posterior Distribution of the Discrete Change Point" in page 126 of the Stan Manual. As described therein, one should normalize the values in the array "lp" to get the probability p(s | e, l, D). This, I get. However, I do not understand why the subsequent equation is true. The summation in this equation is an approximation of E(p(s, D | e, l)), right? [[Here E stands for expectation, which is taken over the posterior p(e, l | D).]]

I don't see why this equals to p(s | D). Isn't the quantity p(s | D) actually equal to E(p(s | e, l, D))? [[Again, the expectation is taken over the posterior p(e, l | D).]] It seems to me that these two expectations are not the same, since p(s, D | e, l) = p(s | e, l, D) * p(D | e, l) whose second term is non-constant within the said expectations.

By not correcting for the term p(D | e, l), doesn't the summation "skip" the per-iteration normalization discussed earlier in the paragraph? Where am I going wrong? Or, is there an error in this subsection of the Stan Manual?

Thanks,

Mehmet Ozan Kabak

PS. I am new to Stan, but I love it already. Big thanks to the team for making it available to the world.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A question about the Change Point Model example in the manual
parts:
I'm confused about where you're talking about.

If I'm looking at the right equation, there are no
expectations involved --- it's just computing the
likelihood function by marginalizing out the cutpoint.
And it's just using the usual law of total probability
to do it:

p(D | e, l) = SUM_s p(s, D | e, l) [ law of total probability ]

= SUM_s p(s) p(D | e, l) [ definition of joint probability ]

and then the prior p(s) and the likelihood p(D | e, l) break
down into their own terms.

So I don't know what you mean by correcting for the term p(D | e, l).
We don't ever need to compute p(s | D).

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] A question about the Change Point Model example in the manual
parts:
Sorry --- thought I'd written back.

That was confusing how I wrote it. The point is that
we're defining q(s | D), which isn't normalized, then just
normalizing it by dividing each entry by the sum; see
the following formula on p. 127.

On the log scale, that amounts to subtracting log_sum_exp(lp)
from each entry.

I tracked down my original code and I just did the normalization
in R using my own function:

log_softmax <- function(x) {
z <- exp(x - max(x));
return(log(z / sum(z)));
}

And it's not even good R code --- that last line should
be log(z) - log(sum(z)) for arithmetic stability.

I should've added the code direclty within the Stan generated quantities
block (I may have done it in R). I'll do that going forward.
See:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1709#issuecomment-172069425

- Bob
